The deadline to apply is Monday, January 31. Council members chose to seek applications for appointment to City Council from residents to serve as interim council member until the results of the general municipal election are certified on November 8. Residents must meet three requirements to apply for the position: 1. Must be a qualified registered voter in Piedmont 2. Must not hold any other office or employment with the city 3. Must not be rendered ineligible due to the term limits provisions of the City Charter Interested residents may submit applications electronically, or in-person to the City Clerk’s Office by 5 p.m. on January 31. Postmarks will not be accepted. Members of the city council will interview candidates at which time applicants will have the opportunity to discuss their candidacy with council members. At a special meeting on February 7 applicants will be asked to make a brief presentation to council members. Piedmont Mayor Teddy Gray King noted at the January 6 meeting that this is the third time she has assisted in filling a vacancy mid-election. City Council filled vacancies left by former mayor Margaret Fujioka in 2016 and former mayor Jeff Wieler in 2017. The Council also chose to take applications from residents in those appointments. “Both times resulted in finding new talent [for City Council],” said King. Applications are available on the City website at https://piedmont.ca.gov and from the City Clerk’s Office. articles.text: Piedmont students started their second semester of classes on Wednesday, January 5, but not all of them were in school, likely due to a surge in Covid-19 cases spurred on by the Omicron variant. Attendance the first three days back was down by approximately 10% through the district compared to the last week of class in December. The district, with an estimated enrollment of 2413 in its six schools, has reported that approximately 228 covid cases were reported among staff and students between December 17 and January 10. An estimated 190 cases were reported to the district prior to the resumption of classes on January 5. In comparison, in the first four months of the school year only 24 student cases and 13 staff cases were recorded. “With the need for testing and backlog of emails and voicemails for our District nurses and Health Clerks, the decision was made to prioritize clearing students and staff to return to campus,” said Communications Director Brian Killgore.” “While we can attribute some of these absences to positive COVID cases, we are aware of families keeping their students home as a precaution,” Killgore said. Students weren’t the only ones missing from campus. There were 27 staff absences on Wednesday, the first day back, 34 absences Thursday and Friday, and 35 on Monday, January 10. “We want to be clear this does not mean every absent staff member has tested positive for Covid. Some may have symptoms and stayed home as a precaution, or were absent for other reasons, such as staying home with a sick child,” Killgore said. With substitutes and other district staff member filling in, all teacher vacancies were covered through Monday this week, January 10. Finding available substitutes has been a problem all year across the country, prompting the Piedmont School District to increase the per diem rate for substitutes in September from $140 to $200 a day. articles.text: After a lifetime of my typical fare of taco truck burritos, Smokehouse hamburgers and quesadilla tacos, I was finally sitting down to a dinner of elegant French food in a fine bistro in Menlo Park with our friends and former Piedmonters Bob and Dianne Coleman. Right after the French onion soup arrived, things got ugly and fast. Seems like after years of abuse my gall bladder had chosen this moment to go on strike. After a few minutes of considering whether it was just food poisoning, it became evident that I was seriously sick. After a few hours of trying to wait it out back home, and consulting with our neighbors and friends Mike and Drennan, we made our way down to Alta Bates Hospital emergency room. Mike is an EMT and I seriously recommend everyone have an EMT friend down the street. Four hours later they got me in to see the doctor who, after tests, said “You have a gangrenous gall bladder and it needs to come out, now. “I have always been a procrastinator – fast decisions are not my style – but this seemed the time for action. So, despite the fact that my surgeon looked like Ferris Buehler, none of the hospital staff had seen or heard of him, and there was no internet in the emergency room to check any reviews, off we went. Back in my room I met my nurse, a middle-aged man from Nigeria named Gracious, and another nurse, a young lady from Ethiopia named Lovely. They wrote their names on the whiteboard on the wall along with my name and the date. I liked looking up and seeing them. Psalm 23 says “surely goodness and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life…” Gracious and Lovely is not bad either. Thank God for the miracle of anesthesia. I remember nothing of the surgery except for a few seconds of the surgeon’s choice of 70’s rock and roll as operating music before blacking out. Back in a regular room I was introduced to my roommate, Josh. Usually you would think a private room would be better than a shared one, but not with Josh. My new golden hair-streaked millennial hipster friend was there to show me the ropes. He wanted a sandwich and they declined as it was too close to his surgery time. “Cancel the surgery,” he calmly said. They gave him the sandwich and the surgery. When breakfast arrived and was inedible, he immediately called the nurse and ordered French toast and scrambled eggs. “Make it two” I yelled. When things got a little slow in the evening he called and ordered Door Dash to deliver two milkshakes and 4 cookies from The Creamery. Who knew you could do that? When it was time for his elbow surgery and he put on the backless gown, he asked for pants to go with it. They came immediately. I had no idea there was an alternative to flashing your backside down the hallway. Later I said to Josh through the curtain that divided our beds, “Josh how did you get to know so much about hospitals?” “Four years ago I had leukemia and spent quite a bit of time in them. This one’s OK but I have seen better. You should try the UC Hospitals – their desserts are amazing.” Wherever you are now Josh, thanks. You were a gracious gift and made my one night in the hospital a memorable one. Bill McNabb is the former Senior Minister at Piedmont community Church and a longtime Piedmont resident. articles.text: We are in a battle on many fronts. That much is clear as we begin 2022. Medically, we are in a battle to subdue COVID-19. Politically, we are in a battle to preserve democracy. Religiously, we are in a battle to keep Christ in Christianity. Thus, television series like “The Mandlorian” offer meaningful reflection on the world we live in, raising questions such as how we best wage the battles of our time. One of those questions is, “Are we better off keeping our helmets on or taking them off?” If, like me, you watch the series, then you know that the title character, following the Way of the Mandalores, neither takes off his helmet nor allows it to be removed by others. There are reasons practical (the helmet provides protection) and spiritual (“This is the Way”) for this practice. However, as the story unfolds, it becomes clear that practitioners of the Way are far from united in this practice. Some, like the more fanatical Children of the Watch, forbid the removal of one’s helmet with few exceptions. Others, such as the storied anti-Imperial warrior Bo-Katan, take off their helmet whenever they please. For 24 years, Piedmont residents have made sure their travels are well documented, with photos of family members reading the Piedmont Post in far-off places throughout the world, and some nearby. The Post invites families to send photos with the Post from near and far for publication in Where in the World Are We on the back page of the paper. With people able to travel once again, there is no better time to have your photo in the Post. Send photos as jpg. files to: news@piedmontpost.org, and be sure to include a brief description of the location where the photo was taken.

articles.text: The Piedmont Planning Commission discussed aspects of Senate Bill (SB) 9 at a January 10 meeting and how it will apply to the city’s fair housing endeavors. “The state has decided that cities are not processing construction of new housing units fast enough. So [the city] can only provide objective standards, much like a building code is an objective standard, and there can be no discretion in the review. This is a major change,” said Senior Piedmont Planner Pierce Macdonald-Powell. SB 9 was signed into law by Gov. Gavin Newsom in September 2021, and the requirements of the bill went into effect on January 1 of this year. It requires local jurisdictions to grant by-right approval of housing developments of one to two units, and urban lot ‘splits’ for single-family zoning districts. “SB 9 is a state law we’re going to have to address in the city zoning code,” Piedmont Planning Director Kevin Jackson confirmed. In Piedmont, single-family zoning districts are Zone A and E. Homeowners in these zones would be eligible to split their lot into a duplex-style, or two properties on one lot, if it involves the demolition of no more than 25% of the exterior walls or structure. The result would be two parcels of approximately equal size. The secondary ‘property’ may be then used for home ownership, or to rent out to a tenant that will occupy the property for more than 30 days. Short-term rentals, like for popular rental websites AirBnB or VRBO, are not permitted. The new structure would not need a design review permit. “That is the crux of SB 9,” said Macdonald-Powell confirmed. Jackson explained that the city will need to develop objective design standards for projects that are eligible for SB 9. Units and subdivisions created under SB 9 would not be reviewed by the Planning Commission, would not be subject to public hearing or right of appeal, and must be reviewed by city staff according to objective standards, not yet created by the city. The law is not specific about whether or not the lots created could also have Accessory Dwelling Units (ADUs) or Junior Accessory Dwelling Units (JADUs) in addition to those two lots, Macdonald-Powell added.
articles.title: How will Senate Bill 9 affect Piedmont and its housing future?

articles.text: The Piedmont City Council rejected a recommendation to increase the speed limit on Moraga Avenue from 25 mph to 30 mph at a December 20, 2021 meeting. A study done by Kittelson & Associates, Inc. was presented to council members, which included the recommendation of raising the speed limit on Moraga Avenue from Ramona Avenue to Maxwelton Road – its entire length in the city of Piedmont – by 5 mph. The city asked Kittelson & Associates to complete a study on selective roads to ensure compliance with state regulations. Speed limits throughout Piedmont have been established over the years by traffic and radar speed studies. “We get speed complaints on Moraga Avenue, and we’re considering installing [Class II] bike lanes on Moraga around Coaches Field, as well as doing striping modifications. Both of those, we feel, will have a positive impact in reducing speeds through that area,” City Planner John Wanger said. Between 2016 and 2021 there have been 32 collisions on Moraga Avenue. Police Chief Jeremy Bowers added that radar enforcement could not be used for this stretch of Moraga Avenue if the speed limit remains at 25 mph. Bowers confirmed that the department does receive speed complaints, and that the department would address complaints in different ways. The city council adopted all other findings and recommendations in the Speed Zone Engineering and Traffic Study conducted by Kittelson & Associates, Inc., dated August 2021. The survey included 12 non-residential roadway segments in Piedmont.

articles.text: The League of California Cities, a non-profit statewide association that provides education and training services to elected city officials, released a report detailing legislation passed last year and how it will affect cities across the state. The League zeroed in on Senate Bill (SB) 9, which requires local governments to approve housing developments containing two residential units in single-family zones and urban lot splits. The report found that lawmakers introduced 2,421 bills total, far surpassing the totals of 2019 and 2020. Of the 836 bills to reach the governor’s desk, about 92% were signed into law, many of which made a significant investment in the production of affordable housing. However, more than 240 cities joined the League in its opposition of SB 9 before Gov. Newsom signed it into law in September 2021. “SB 9 undermines the ability of local governments to responsibly plan for the type of housing that communities need, while usurping local democracy and the input of local residents,” said Carolyn Coleman, CEO of the League of California Cities. The bill was authored by Senate President pro tempore Toni Atkins (D-San Diego), who said it would “set California’s housing availability on a path of inclusion so that more families can attain the California dream.” It was a critical piece of the Senate’s “Housing Package,” a comprehensive effort to increase the state’s affordable housing stock. Assembly member Buffy Wicks, who represents Piedmont in the State Assembly, said that single-family zoning is an exclusionary policy. She was a staunch proponent of SB 9. “Single-family zoning is rooted in redlining. It has created huge problems, and results in exclusionary housing. At least in this bill, these units can be deed-restricted, should local governments decide - which I think is an important step forward,” Wicks said. “We need to legalize duplexes. This bill will create more housing, and density in a way that doesn’t fundamentally alter the character of the neighborhood.” The bill went into effect on January 1 this year, and Bay Area city planners have already received proposals. The City of Concord received its first application under the new bill on January 5. Piedmont has not yet received an application under SB 9. Lic. articles.text: A deadly apartment-building fire in the Bronx, New York last weekend has prompted communities nationwide to revisit safety concerns surrounding electric space heaters. The commonly used appliance was the source of the fire that killed at least 17 people on January 9. A space heater is an appliance that is used to heat a single, small-to-medium sized living area. Although convenient, they can be dangerous if not used properly. The National Fire Protection Association [NFPA] reported in January 2021 that nearly half of all home heating fires occur in December, January, and February, and that heating equipment is the leading cause of fires in homes nationwide. Local fire departments responded to an estimated 48,530 fires involving heating equipment and space heaters every year between 2014 and 2019. “In my experience, fires in living spaces increase during cold winter months,” Piedmont Fire Chief Dave Brannigan confirmed. “Common causes are improperly used or maintained space heaters, floor heaters, and candles. However, fires can be caused by many sources. It’s especially important not to use extension cords with heat producing appliances such as space heaters as they can easily overheat and cause a fire.” It is important to note that, no matter what space heater you own, you should never keep any flammable object within three feet of heating equipment – furnaces, fireplaces, wood stoves, and portable heaters. Portable heaters should be turned off whenever leaving the room or going to bed, and should be placed on a solid, flat surface. Never use space heaters as supplemental clothing dryers – do not place socks, towels, or any other fabric items near the heater. If you have a fuel-burning space heater, use only the fuel type specified by the manufacturer. If you are planning on buying a space heater, choose one that has advanced features to include automatic shut-offs and protection against tipping over. NFPA provides resources for learning more, including informational videos for children, on its website https://www.nfpa.org/ heating. open every day 8:30 am – 3 pm

articles.text: As a family, encourage kids’ creativity. I’m sitting here in the midst of the Omicron surge trying to find words for parents and kids out there on creativity and imagination that could be fun, helpful or inspirational, but I’ve got to admit…the page is feeling awfully blank right now. So, to all the parents out there right now feeling tired and worn out, I just want to say, “I see you.” I read a NY Times piece on their app recently about how we should all just prepare to get back to the world of hours and hours of screen time and be ok with it because that’s just where we are, and I definitely wanted to throw my phone across the room. Anyone else experiencing COVID rage? But, time marches forward and our kids still need us and they need creativity and imagination, so here are a few ideas that are just back to the basics for bringing creative play into your home. music!! Try adding variety by playing with genre: classical, rock, pop, musicals, opera, jazz, big band, all the types of music you can think of or search for on Spotify. 2. Dance/Move You know the dance move “the shopping cart”? Well, have you tried “the tooth brushing?” What about “the eating spaghetti” or “the riding your bike?” Any of these normal day-to-day activities can be turned into dance moves with a little fun and rhythm. Just mime the activity and repeat! Challenge your kids to a “dance off” with these silly movements. 3. Crayon Self Portraits Get out the crayons, put everyone in front of a hand mirror and start to draw. If you want to have some fun with older kids, ask them to try to do the project with their non-dominant hand. 4. Cake Decorating Find all of the weird old jars of sprinkles and decorations that you have sitting around the house. Bake a cake (I highly recommend the one from the box), get your kids to frost it with some store-bought frosting and then let them loose with whatever edible decoration you have in the back of your pantry. 5. Read a Good Book Together (or watch a show based on a good book) I love curling up with kids to read aloud. A lot of parents do this at bedtime, but maybe a rainy Saturday afternoon can also become a book moment. What’s a favorite book from your childhood? Share that with your family. Or, if you are too tired, find a show or a movie based on a book and watch that together. Stories are universal and a great way to escape together into imagination. Nina Meehan is CEO of Bay Area Children’s Theatre. For information see Bay Area Children’s Theatre – Sparking Creativity, Inspiring Imagination (bactheatre.org)

articles.text: For decades the number one impetus for moving to Piedmont has been its schools. But how well compensated are the teachers? A Special School Board meeting was held last week on Thursday, January 6, at which the school board approved a pay increase of 2.5% for all teachers retroactive to July 1, 2021. Based upon information from 2019, teacher salaries can range from approximately $50,000 for a first-year faculty member to a high of around $109,000 (before benefits or extra pay) for a teacher with more than 25 years of experience. A 2.5% increase would see those amounts increase to $51,250 and $111,725. Data on salaries are available for all school district employees of all California public schools. Piedmont School District salaries are available going back only to 2019. Piedmont teachers have received salary increases as follows: 2018-19 3% 2019-20 2% 2020-21 6% 2021-22 2.5% Veteran Piedmont High School English teacher Dr. Elise Marks took over as president of the Associated Piedmont Teachers (APT) at the end of October 2021. The job of president has seen a significant increase in Seen here teaching remotely, Dr. Elise Marks taught an extra class period of English last year due to staffing shortages and is now the APT President. responsibilities since the start of the pandemic, with changes in work environment, safety concerns and general uncertainty. Marks applauded the recent salary agreement with the school district but has warned that inflation is on track to outpace the raises. “The Legislative Analyst’s Office is predicting inflation of 5.35% for next year, and teachers are very worried. One member told me almost half her monthly income is already going to her $1400 rent, which will increase again in January. Others tell me they don’t know how they’re going to manage to keep paying for daycare for their kids,” Marks said.
articles.title: A perspective on teacher raises

By Nina Meehan I’m sitting here in the midst of the Omicron surge trying to find words for parents and kids out there on creativity and imagination that could be fun, helpful or inspirational, but I’ve got to admit…the page is feeling awfully blank right now. So, to all the parents out there right now feeling tired and worn out, I just want to say, “I see you.” I read a NY Times piece on their app recently about how we should all just prepare to get back to the world of hours and hours of screen time and be ok with it because that’s just where we are, and I definitely wanted to throw my phone across the room. Anyone else experiencing COVID rage? But, time marches forward and our kids still need us and they need creativity and imagination, so here are a few ideas that are just back to the basics for bringing creative play into your home. Back to the Basics 1. Play Music In the car, in the kitchen, during bath time, turn up the music!! Try adding variety by playing with genre: classical, rock, pop, musicals, opera, jazz, big band, all the types of music you can think of or search for on Spotify. 2. Dance/Move You know the dance move “the shopping cart”? Well, have you tried “the tooth brushing?” What about “the eating spaghetti” or “the riding your bike?” Any of these normal day-to-day activities can be turned into dance moves with a little fun and rhythm. Just mime the activity and repeat! Challenge your kids to a “dance off” with these silly movements. 3. Crayon Self Portraits Get out the crayons, put everyone in front of a hand mirror and start to draw. If you want to have some fun with older kids, ask them to try to do the project with their non-dominant hand. 4. Cake Decorating Find all of the weird old jars of sprinkles and decorations that you have sitting around the house. A lot of parents do this at bedtime, but maybe a rainy Saturday afternoon can also become a book moment. What’s a favorite book from your childhood? Share that with your family. Or, if you are too tired, find a show or a movie based on a book and watch that together. Stories are universal and a great way to escape together into imagination. articles.text: This Christmas break, my dad decided to entertain the family by renting a house near Lake Tahoe. We hadn’t seen snow for a while, and most of us were excited to do some skiing. It should be noted that the family skiing aptitude is not distributed equally. My dad is a world record holder in high hurdles, so he’s pretty good with keeping his balance. My older sister and her boyfriend (also invited) both played sports in high school. I did cross-country running. It doesn’t help much when it comes to doing cross-country skiing, but it’s something. Lastly, my mother, who hadn’t done any sports before meeting my dad, has skied once or twice – and without much enthusiasm, I should add. On the second day of our stay at Tahoe, the five of us dressed in the ridiculously bulky ski clothes, piled into the car and drove to North Tahoe Cross Country. As we waited for our skis at the rental counter, our anticipation was building. Six years ago we tried skiing and struggled getting our skis on without them falling off when we tried to lift our feet. To get to the trails this winter we struggled up a steep hill – kind of the opposite of what most cross-country skiers expect. But after that, nothing could stop us, at least that’s what we thought. For a while I was in the lead, showing off to the stragglers behind me. But then I got too cocky and fell as I tried to go faster. The real challenge was to get up: after making positions I didn’t even know I could do, I pulled myself up, only to start sliding down the hill. I remembered hearing about the “the pizza method” (also known as the snowplow), in which you point your skis towards each other to slow your descent. That helped me stop, but now I had to go back up the hill. After my less than graceful descent down the first hill, everything was calm. My sister, mother, and I were going steady, while my dad and my sister’s boyfriend were speeding ahead. The forest around us was beautiful; all the evergreens were covered in snow, like a Nutcracker wonderland. In about an hour, we stopped for a water break. Looking at a map of the trails, my dad figured out that the next portion was downhill. I led the charge, and when I saw the sign “To Lodge” I assumed that’s where we were going before anything bad happened (think Donner Party). But instead, the Edel Party decided to push ahead to find a lake my mother claimed she remembered from six years earlier. I, on the other hand, wished them good luck and headed to warmth and safety. After my share of humiliating falls, I just took off my skis and walked, arriving at the lodge in one piece. And there, after making myself comfortable by the fireplace, I began my wait. Thirty minutes went by, then forty, and still no sign of anyone. Finally, I got a call from my dad saying he was almost at the lodge, and could I please ask the front desk to arrange a lift for my mom? I was confused – what happened to my mom and the rest of the family? Arriving in a few minutes, my dad explained that after a bad downhill fall that had wiped out all four of them, my mom lost her confidence, and as the saying goes, it really went downhill for her from there. On her last fall, she had injured her knee, so my dad had gone ahead to get help. Soon, in came the hobbling hero at the lodge on her own, somehow having missed the snowmobile that had been dispatched to rescue her. The three of us settled in the warming hut, my mom in a rather gloomy mood. I finally got a text from my sister. She and her boyfriend were still looking for the lake, whose existence at that point sounded very suspicious. Inspecting the map, I came to the conclusion that the only possible “lake” around there was a scenic lookout with a view of Lake Tahoe. I sent the photo of the map to my sister, who by now was completely lost. She and her boyfriend had to retrace their steps for 45 minutes, then spend another hour skiing to the lodge. When they finally arrived, they were barely walking – or talking. Next came a trip to the pharmacy for ice packs for my mom’s knee, and phone calls to various orthopedists. The weather forecast kept flashing winter storm warnings, and while my sister and her boyfriend did choose to go downhill skiing the next day, my mother packed our bags and reminisced about driving in a snowstorm in the Alps. Her terrifying stories had some effect on my dad. On the morning of our departure, we left the earliest we ever had in the history of the Edel family. Slowly, we made our way across the barely visible Donner Pass on slippery mountain roads. In retrospect, I love being outdoors in the snow, but I think I’ve had my fill of snow for the next couple of years. Larissa Edel is a freshman at Bentley School in Lafayette.

articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. The Post will publish the weekly street sweeping schedule from now through February, 2022. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. From traditional ground burial and services, to cremation and more progressive services, whatever your needs are, we are here to help you. articles.text: Parents, public not told until January Staff Photos Piedmont High School made a decision in December to not renew the contract of football head coach Jerome Johnson. Staff Photos Jerome Johnson’s departure means Piedmont will lose former NFL running back Jarmar Julien as its offensive coordinator. Piedmont High School has declined to renew the year-toyear contract with head football coach Jerome Johnson after a season marked by an unusually low turnout of players. Johnson, with 30 years of experience as a football coach, departs after building a 10-14 overall record in three seasons. His team was 5-0 in the shortened spring season of 2021 but witnessed an historic low turnout of players last fall, August 2021. The varsity ended up with barely 20 players, though the JV team had a reasonably healthy turnout of players. But playing a full schedule of games this past fall with a shallow roster meant that the majority of players played a full game on both offense and defense. The overall effect of fatigue led directly to a 2-7 season record. It has been confirmed that Johnson was let go on December 3, though the school made no announcement. It appears that the first notification to football parents was an e-mail sent by Athletic Director Bradley Smet on January 7 inviting them to a virtual meeting three days later on Monday, January 10. Parents tuning in to the meeting on zoom expressed shock at the decision and the school’s lack of effort to inform them of the decision and the future of the sport at PHS. The school has made no announcement to parents or the public on its plans for the search for new head coach. It also has not confirmed plans for the future in general of football at Piedmont High School. The school was one of the first in the East to establish a football program, dating back to 1921 when the high school was built. Sudden and sometimes inexplicable coaching changes are part of the recent history of the school’s athletic department, and the school has built a reputation among coaches a being unstable. Johnson’s firing is reminiscent of the release of basketball coaches Mike Hudson in 2020, and Chris Lavdiotis in 2018. Hudson is now head coach at Berkeley, and Lavdiotis is head girls coach at Miramonte. The sacking of Jerem Stothers as head coach of the boys’ lacrosse team in 2016 is another example of a successful coach abruptly shown the door. Stothers takes over as Berkeley’s head coach this spring. The PHS varsity football program took a major hit in roster size last fall resulting in a roster of as few as 14 players, as opposed to 35-40 in a normal year. Going into its last game of the season, Piedmont was 2-3 against league opponents based upon a strong defensive unit. But with injuries building up as players had to compensate for a reduced roster by playing both offense and defense, Johnson was placed in an impossible situation. The future looked bright for the JV program, but only five seniors were expected to be available on the team next fall. Johnson came to the school as an assistant under head coach John Trotman in 2019. He was promoted to head coach after Trotman accepted a fulltime job and some job stability with the San Francisco Department of Public Health. Johnson was the Defensive Coordinator at McClymonds when it won the State Championship in 2016. He was a member of the coaching staff at Bishop O’Dowd led by Hardy Nickerson from 2010-2013. He was also Contra Costa College’s director of football operations under Alonzo Carter, now San Jose State’s running back’s coach and assistant head coach. Piedmont posted a 3-7 record in Johnson’s first season at Piedmont with a roster comprised of mostly Junior Varsity call-ups, largely juniors. After a summer and fall without football due to the global pandemic, the same roster returned in the spring of 2021 for its shortened season, going a perfect 5-0. Johnson’s dismissal comes as the latest chapter in what continues to be seen as an incoherent athletic department.

articles.text: Following the news this week of Piedmont High School’s decision on December 3 to not renew the contract of head football coach Jerome Johnson, parents and students are left to ask what the future holds for the sport. Football and track are the oldest sports at Piedmont High, both actively competing since the school’s founding in 1921. But does a 100-year tradition have any meaning? THE SCHOOL HAS NOT The school has not yet announced to the pubic the dismissal of coach Johnson, nor has it announced a plan to hire new coaches, or even plans for the football season next fall. Faced with a drastically low turnout of varsity-level players this past fall, the school seemed to make no attempt to gather parents and students during the season to hatch a plan to have a sufficient number or juniors and seniors interested in playing football come August 2020. Parents of JV payers have been fully supportive of efforts to build the program in the past year and a half. But no effort appears to have been made during the season, nor immediately after its conclusion. No meeting with parents seems to have been scheduled in October or November, and the question of the future of football at Witter Field was barely touched upon at the team’s end-of-season banquet. Many football parents were blindsided by an announcement from Athletic Director Bradley Smet on January 7 that a meeting of parents would be held on January 10. The meeting was ostensibly to discuss the future of the program, but for some parents it was the first time they learned that Johnson was terminated as head coach on December 3, one month earlier. This comes after initial roster numbers suggest 32 players would be available, while other projections propose the number is closer to 38 students spread between Varsity and Junior Varsity. Piedmont’s current options include generating enough interest among student to field a bona fide varsity, settling for a junior varsity team, rebuilding with a Frosh-Soph and a JV team. A Piedmont team would likely play in the Mission Division of the Western Alameda County Conference and compete in the Shoreline Division, the least competitive group of schools. Piedmont would play some favorable teams on the mend, like Irvington, Kennedy, Newark Memorial, San Lorenzo, American, Alameda, and Arroyo. Parents and coaches have speculated that the low turnout of players was based primarily on the concern of parents about the health of their students during a time of COVID and its many implications. Coming by Witter Field on a Friday night, the energy from the football crowd is always more boisterous than any other sport at the school, even inside Binks Rawlings Gym for basketball. The tradition of varsity football at Witter goes back to 1921, a history that is rivaled by few.

Johnson, with 30 years of experience as a football coach, departs after building a 10-14 overall record in three seasons. His team was 5-0 in the shortened spring season of 2021 but witnessed an historic low turnout of players last fall, August 2021. The varsity ended up with barely 20 players, though the JV team had a reasonably healthy turnout of players. But playing a full schedule of games this past fall with a shallow roster meant that the majority of players played a full game on both offense and defense. The overall effect of fatigue led directly to a 2-7 season record. It has been confirmed that Johnson was let go on December 3, though the school made no announcement. It appears that the first notification to football parents was an e-mail sent by Athletic Director Bradley Smet on January 7 inviting them to a virtual meeting three days later on Monday, January 10. Parents tuning in to the meeting on zoom expressed shock at the decision and the school’s lack of effort to inform them of the decision and the future of the sport at PHS. The school has made no announcement to parents or the public on its plans for the search for new head coach. It also has not confirmed plans for the future in general of football at Piedmont High School. The school was one of the first in the East to establish a football program, dating back to 1921 when the high school was built. Sudden and sometimes inexplicable coaching changes are part of the recent history of the school’s athletic department, and the school has built a reputation among coaches a being unstable. Johnson’s firing is reminiscent of the release of basketball coaches Mike Hudson in 2020, and Chris Lavdiotis in 2018. Hudson is now head coach at Berkeley, and Lavdiotis is head girls coach at Miramonte. The sacking of Jerem Stothers as head coach of the boys’ lacrosse team in 2016 is another example of a successful coach abruptly shown the door. Stothers takes over as Berkeley’s head coach this spring. The PHS varsity football program took a major hit in roster size last fall resulting in a roster of as few as 14 players, as opposed to 35-40 in a normal year. Going into its last game of the season, Piedmont was 2-3 against league opponents based upon a strong defensive unit. But with injuries building up as players had to compensate for a reduced roster by playing both offense and defense, Johnson was placed in an impossible situation. The future looked bright for the JV program, but only five seniors were expected to be available on the team next fall. Johnson came to the school as an assistant under head coach John Trotman in 2019. He was promoted to head coach after Trotman accepted a fulltime job and some job stability with the San Francisco Department of Public Health. Johnson was the Defensive Coordinator at McClymonds when it won the State Championship in 2016. He was a member of the coaching staff at Bishop O’Dowd led by Hardy Nickerson from 2010-2013. He was also Contra Costa College’s director of football operations under Alonzo Carter, now San Jose State’s running back’s coach and assistant head coach. Piedmont posted a 3-7 record in Johnson’s first season at Piedmont with a roster comprised of mostly Junior Varsity call-ups, largely juniors. After a summer and fall without football due to the global pandemic, the same roster returned in the spring of 2021 for its shortened season, going a perfect 5-0. Johnson’s dismissal comes as the latest chapter in what continues to be seen as an incoherent athletic department. What is the future of football at Piedmont High? Pattern of dysfunction in Athletic Dept. continues as head coach is released By Jonathan Comeaux Following the news this week of Piedmont High School’s decision on December 3 to not renew the contract of head football coach Jerome Johnson, parents and students are left to ask what the future holds for the sport. Football and track are the oldest sports at Piedmont High, both actively competing since the school’s founding in 1921. But does a 100-year tradition have any meaning? THE SCHOOL HAS NOT The school has not yet announced to the pubic the dismissal of coach Johnson, nor has it announced a plan to hire new coaches, or even plans for the football season next fall. Faced with a drastically low turnout of varsity-level players this past fall, the school seemed to make no attempt to gather parents and students during the season to hatch a plan to have a sufficient number or juniors and seniors interested in playing football come August 2020. Parents of JV payers have been fully supportive of efforts to build the program in the past year and a half. But no effort appears to have been made during the season, nor immediately after its conclusion. No meeting with parents seems to have been scheduled in October or November, and the question of the future of football at Witter Field was barely touched upon at the team’s end-of-season banquet. Many football parents were blindsided by an announcement from Athletic Director Bradley Smet on January 7 that a meeting of parents would be held on January 10. The meeting was ostensibly to discuss the future of the program, but for some parents it was the first time they learned that Johnson was terminated as head coach on December 3, one month earlier. This comes after initial roster numbers suggest 32 players would be available, while other projections propose the number is closer to 38 students spread between Varsity and Junior Varsity. Piedmont’s current options include generating enough interest among student to field a bona fide varsity, settling for a junior varsity team, rebuilding with a Frosh-Soph and a JV team. A Piedmont team would likely play in the Mission Division of the Western Alameda County Conference and compete in the Shoreline Division, the least competitive group of schools. Piedmont would play some favorable teams on the mend, like Irvington, Kennedy, Newark Memorial, San Lorenzo, American, Alameda, and Arroyo. Parents and coaches have speculated that the low turnout of players was based primarily on the concern of parents about the health of their students during a time of COVID and its many implications. Coming by Witter Field on a Friday night, the energy from the football crowd is always more boisterous than any other sport at the school, even inside Binks Rawlings Gym for basketball. Now, after the recent rains, the area near Sunol, is lively again and is in its prime stages of activity. The area is among the smaller of East Bay Regional Park District’s parks but is also one of the more popular destinations with its creek and rocky terrain Little Yosemite. It becomes a frequented watering hole in the warmer months, while those seeking a jolt will still find a reason to jump in the water this winter. The location is a bit of a beginners’ course in canyon climbing as you scale over boulders, keeping sharp eyes on where to put feet, hands, and track landing spots. The rocks require proper footwear and grip, given some of the stones have compiled algae and are quite slippery. The walk from the Sunol Regional parking lot is a mellow 1.1 miles from the gate on Ohlone Road. Given its popularity, you’ll see plenty of people. Adjacent to the main trail is a more secluded path along the creek, eventually re-merging with Ohlone Road on your way to Little Yosemite. The path down to the Little Yosemite area is narrow, and depending on the time of the day and year, you will likely be taking your time. On our 1.1-mile hike toward Little Yosemite, we saw 77 other hikers on a Sunday morning, despite using the more secluded portion of the trail for half of the walk. On the walk back on the main trail, we saw 155 other walkers including a large number of families.

articles.text: After missing time before the start of the winter break due to an ankle injury, senior Jojo Murphy was back on the court and clearly ready to play on January 5. He led the Highlanders to an impressive 62-42 victory over Berkeley, with a double-double performance – 20 points and 12 rebounds, in addition to four steals and three assists. Playing in front of a hometown crowd at Binks Rawlings Gym, the dynamic duo of Murphy and A.J. Harris – who had 14 points and eight boards – led the offense, while Piedmont’s vaunted defense held the Yellowjackets to less than 10 points in each of the final two quarters. “It was great to be back,” said Murphy. “We put a lot of work in and have fought a lot of adversity already this year with coaches being gone and a lot of injuries. It felt great to be back out here with the guys. There’s nothing I love more than to be out here and playing ball. “I did a lot of recovery work for two weeks, working out on the bike, dribbling, and shooting exercises to just keep my game polished,” he added. “I thought tonight was good because we responded well in the second half. We went into halftime with a four-point lead, then played good defense and kept our composure. I think we grew as a team tonight,” said coach Jason Harris. The game was its first against a league opponent in the Foothill Division of the Western Alameda County Conference. Piedmont’s defense shut down Berkeley, holding the visitors to eight points each in the third and fourth quarters. “One of coach Ben Spencer’s mantras is to allow only 10 points a quarter. articles.text: Former Music Director Michael Tilson Thomas (MTT) will conduct the San Francisco Symphony in two weeks of concerts live at Davies Symphony Hall. The first concerts, held January 20 through 22 will include Prokofiev’s Symphony No. 5 and Shostakovich’s Cello Concerto No. 2 with guest cellist Gautier Capucon. Concerts from January 27 through 29 will feature Gustav Mahler’s Symphony No. 1, and pianist Yuja Wang performing Franz Liszt’s Piano Concerto No. 1. Tilson Thomas became Music Director of the San Francisco Symphony in 1995, during a period of significant growth and recognition of the orchestra. He led the symphony in championing contemporary and American composers alongside classical masters and continues to lead the orchestra in four weeks of concerts annually. Tickets for concerts at Davies Symphony Hall can be purchased at www.sfsymphony.org, or by calling the box office at (415) Michael Tilson Thomas 864-6000. Davies Symphony Hall is located at 201 Van Ness Avenue in San Francisco. New health protocols as of February 1 San Francisco Symphony announced updated safety protocols on January 4 for audiences attending live performances at Davies Symphony Hall. Beginning February 1, proof of a COVID-19 booster received at least one week prior to an event will be required for entrances into the symphony hall. The announcement expands the symphony’s already established requirement that all patrons, performers, volunteers, and staff age 12 and up present proof of vaccination against COVID-19 for entry into Davies Symphony Hall and all events held at that venue. Audience members younger than 12 may show proof of vaccination or a negative COVID-19 test. Audience members age 2 to 4 must show proof of a negative COVID- 19 test. PCR tests may be shown within 48 hours of the event, or an antigen rapid test shown within 24 hours of the event.

articles.text: SF Sketchfest, a comedy and improv festival that was founded in 2001, announced that this year’s event will be postponed to a future date due to the rise of COVID cases in the Bay Area. The festival was originally scheduled to take place January 7 through January 23 at various locations in San Francisco. Festival co-founders Cole Stratton, David Owen, and Janet Varney explained the reasoning for postponement in a festival update listed on the event’s webpage. Many artists have reached out to the co-founders and expressed concern about traveling and performing at a time when the COVID Omicron variant is causing increased positive and breakthrough infections around the country. “We have also had some artists and staff members test positive for COVID,” the announcement explained. “Faced with multiple artists, show, and flight cancellations, we have made the tough decision to postpone the festival to a later date. Our goal is to keep as much of the original lineup intact as possible.” Ticket holders will be contacted directly in the coming weeks with rescheduled dates, details, and options. Questions can be sent to boxoffice@sfsketchfest.com. Visit https://sfsketchfest. com/2022-festival-update/ for more information about the postponement and the event, which is now in its 20th year.

articles.text: Journalist, essayist and screenwriter Joan Didion died on December 23, 2021, leaving behind an expansive portfolio of work that encompasses decades of California history and culture. Her contributions to the field of journalism ushered in a style of writing known as ‘New Journalism,’ reminiscent of long-form non-fiction. Didion, originally from Sacramento, began her career as a journalist in the 1960’s chronicling huge counter-culture movements of her day - most notably the “Hippie counterculture” movement largely headquartered in San Francisco’s Haight-Asbury district. Didion arrived there at the most opportune time to observe the movement – during the height of the “Summer of Love” in 1967. Her observations were published in the September 23, 1967 edition of Saturday Evening Post. Didion reported on what she called “America’s atomization” – the failure of the American Dream, the things America promised but did not deliver, and proof that things fall apart. The fact that her reportage comes mainly from California, where gilded and optimistic interpretations of the American Dream reigned, was nothing short of ironic. Speaking from nativism and experience, she challenged what her contemporaries thought they knew about California, especially her colleagues and editors in New York City. In Where I was From, she describes the Californians she was observing. “They who came to California were not the self-satisfied, happy and content people, but the adventurous, the restless, and the daring, They were different even from those who settled in other western states. They didn’t come west for homes and security, but for adventure and money. They pushed in over the mountains and founded the biggest cities in the west.” Didion can be considered one of the few examples of writers who succeeded in writing for the screen, the novel, and the newspaper. She and her husband John Gregory Dunne wrote over 20 screenplays together, including The Panic in Needle Park, A Star is Born (which was remade to cast Lady Gaga and Bradley Cooper in 2018), and Up Close and Personal. Didion was so influential as a California letter writer that shortly after the announcement of her death, Gov. Gavin Newsom Joan Didion in 2019. Photo by Brigitte Lacombe Photo courtesy of The New Yorker Joan Didion pictured in San Francisco’s Haight-Ashbury district in the 1960s released a lengthy statement eulogizing her as the “requisite voice of California.” “A fifth-generation Californian, Joan was a pioneer of the new journalism movement of the 1960s, capturing in prose the state’s growing counterculture movement that would soon influence the nation,” Newsom wrote. “She was peerless in her capacity to write about life, loss, love and society – easily the best living writer in California. Her ability to put the tapestry of California and the times into words made her a treasure for her generation and generations to come. California belonged to Joan Didion.” For those interested in discovering or revisiting Didion’s work, I would suggest beginning with her debut collection of essays, Slouching Toward Bethlehem. Her novel The Year of Magical Thinking, which won the 2005 National Book Award for Nonfiction, is another must-read. A masterful documentary produced by her nephew Griffin Dunne, entitled The Center Will Not Hold, is available on Netflix. Photo courtesy of New York Times Joan Didion pictured at her house in Malibu with husband John Gregory Dunne, who died in 2003, and their daughter, Quintana Roo Dunne, who died a year and a half later.
articles.title: A dedication to Joan Didion

articles.text: About this time of year, the President delivers the State of the Union address. He tells it like it is – politically. So, what is the state of music? Let me tell you like it is – at least from my standpoint. Almost everyone knows of the Pantheon in Athens. I suggest that we construct a Musical pantheon. And just who should be in our pantheon, you might ask? I suggest that we begin with two surprises from the world of sports. The first person I want in the musical pantheon is the great football coach Vince Lombardi. Why start with coach Lombardi? He was a man of great discipline and integrity. He taught all of his players to be respectful and keep their mind on their business. His famous quote “control the line of scrimmage“ applies very much to music. He did not allow touchdown celebrations. He taught respect. Proof of his success is his winning record and also that his football players went on to lead successful lives after the gridiron. It is good to pattern ourselves after his example. Staying in the world of sports, I select the sports columnist Jim Murray. He didn’t write so much about sports as he saw it. The fact is, he had terrible eyesight. Murray commented on sports more from a philosophical standpoint. His criticism could be biting but it was written in such a way that no one was offended. Modern society has much to learn from people like Jim Murray. Paganini comes next. His accomplishments in music are legendary. He is often considered the greatest violinist of all time. But he was much more than that. He was the prototype for every entertainer who came after him. Without Paganini there would have been no Frank Sinatra, no Elvis, no Beatles, no Mohamed Ali. Paganini invented publicity. I would also include Enrico Caruso, perhaps the greatest tenor of all time. He also had a great work ethic and was a great colleague. Did you know that he was a composer and a famous artist? Jascha Heifetz is in contention as the greatest violinist of all time. Sadly, he is one of the most misunderstood and maligned performers of all time. He was accused of cold and mechanical perfection. This is simply not true. His 100% sincerity was misunderstood as coldness. His mantra was to give his very best at all times or die in the attempt. No performances were identical. He always observed the reactions of the audience. If he felt he was losing the attention of an audience, Green Bay Packers football coach Vince Lombardi. he felt he had to do something out of the ordinary. He said that he deserved to be booed if he didn’t give 100%. Where are artists like these today? Many of the artists of today are far more perfect than those of yesteryear. Violinists of today actually exceed the perfection of Jascha Heifetz. I’ll tell you a little secret; if you listen to some of his recordings, there are places where he really messes up. But he actually wanted those to be included on his recordings. He was human. He had great integrity and sincerity, something I can personally confirm. Today’s players remind me of automatons. They are perfect today, yesterday and ditto tomorrow. Every performance is exactly the same. In the headlong quest for uniform perfection, however, they have lost their humanity. They make up for it with uniformity. Instead of looking within to their souls. We often read in the major newspapers that the musical performer “attacked the instrument”. Attacking the instrument is real big these days. So is “tearing into the instrument”. Loud is good, louder is better, some say. I am reminded of one of the great violinists of the past, Mischa Elman. When he was praised for his powerful tone, Elman always replied the same way: “the violin is not a trumpet. You say I have a big tone. That is only half the story. The other half is that I can play softer than anybody else.” It is that contrast which made Elman so marvelous. How important is nuance to art these days? Unique personalities and national differences made the old performers individual and unique. I much prefer that to the uniformity and predictability of today’s performers. Perfection they have. That is marvelous in its way. But the cost in humanity is lamentable. And so it goes in the world of music.
articles.title: Telling it like it is

In Where I was From, she describes the Californians she was observing. “They who came to California were not the self-satisfied, happy and content people, but the adventurous, the restless, and the daring, They were different even from those who settled in other western states. They didn’t come west for homes and security, but for adventure and money. They pushed in over the mountains and founded the biggest cities in the west.” Didion can be considered one of the few examples of writers who succeeded in writing for the screen, the novel, and the newspaper. She and her husband John Gregory Dunne wrote over 20 screenplays together, including The Panic in Needle Park, A Star is Born (which was remade to cast Lady Gaga and Bradley Cooper in 2018), and Up Close and Personal. Didion was so influential as a California letter writer that shortly after the announcement of her death, Gov. Gavin Newsom By Joseph Gold About this time of year, the President delivers the State of the Union address. He tells it like it is – politically. So, what is the state of music? Let me tell you like it is – at least from my standpoint. Almost everyone knows of the Pantheon in Athens. I suggest that we construct a Musical pantheon. And just who should be in our pantheon, you might ask? I suggest that we begin with two surprises from the world of sports. The first person I want in the musical pantheon is the great football coach Vince Lombardi. Why start with coach Lombardi? He was a man of great discipline and integrity. He taught all of his players to be respectful and keep their mind on their business. His famous quote “control the line of scrimmage“ applies very much to music. He did not allow touchdown celebrations. He taught respect. Proof of his success is his winning record and also that his football players went on to lead successful lives after the gridiron. It is good to pattern ourselves after his example. Staying in the world of sports, I select the sports columnist Jim Murray. He didn’t write so much about sports as he saw it. The fact is, he had terrible eyesight. Murray commented on sports more from a philosophical standpoint. His criticism could be biting but it was written in such a way that no one was offended. Modern society has much to learn from people like Jim Murray. Paganini comes next. His accomplishments in music are legendary. He is often considered the greatest violinist of all time. But he was much more than that. He was the prototype for every entertainer who came after him. Without Paganini there would have been no Frank Sinatra, no Elvis, no Beatles, no Mohamed Ali. Paganini invented publicity. I would also include Enrico Caruso, perhaps the greatest tenor of all time. He also had a great work ethic and was a great colleague. Did you know that he was a composer and a famous artist? Jascha Heifetz is in contention as the greatest violinist of all time. Sadly, he is one of the most misunderstood and maligned performers of all time. He was accused of cold and mechanical perfection. This is simply not true. His 100% sincerity was misunderstood as coldness. His mantra was to give his very best at all times or die in the attempt. No performances were identical. He always observed the reactions of the audience. If he felt he was losing the attention of an audience, Green Bay Packers football coach Vince Lombardi. he felt he had to do something out of the ordinary. He said that he deserved to be booed if he didn’t give 100%. Where are artists like these today? Many of the artists of today are far more perfect than those of yesteryear. Violinists of today actually exceed the perfection of Jascha Heifetz. I’ll tell you a little secret; if you listen to some of his recordings, there are places where he really messes up. They are perfect today, yesterday and ditto tomorrow. Every performance is exactly the same. In the headlong quest for uniform perfection, however, they have lost their humanity. They make up for it with uniformity. Instead of looking within to their souls. We often read in the major newspapers that the musical performer “attacked the instrument”. Attacking the instrument is real big these days. So is “tearing into the instrument”. Loud is good, louder is better, some say. I am reminded of one of the great violinists of the past, Mischa Elman. When he was praised for his powerful tone, Elman always replied the same way: “the violin is not a trumpet. You say I have a big tone. That is only half the story. The other half is that I can play softer than anybody else.” It is that contrast which made Elman so marvelous. How important is nuance to art these days? Unique personalities and national differences made the old performers individual and unique. I much prefer that to the uniformity and predictability of today’s performers. Perfection they have. That is marvelous in its way. But the cost in humanity is lamentable. And so it goes in the world of music. Joan Didion in 2019. articles.text: Gerard Butler and Johnny Wesson star in Chasing Mavericks Chasing Mavericks is a family friendly, classic sports story, reminiscent of those inspirational films that were so ubiquitous in the 70s and 80s. The field of play, however, is not a grassy pitch or an oval track; rather, it’s based on a true story set in a famous surfing spot, just north of Half Moon Bay on the Northern California coast, known for its monster-size 30-foot waves (some peaking over 60 feet) and a dangerous, life threatening undertow. It’s called Mavericks. The focus of the film is a teenager, Jay Moriarity (Johnny Weston), whose dream is to ride the seemingly impossible northern Pacific break. He quickly learns that to ride and survive the El Nino-created waves will require not only extensive training and endurance, but the ability to hold one’s breath for up to four minutes or risk drowning. The narrative opens with 9-year-old Jay attempting to rescue the small dog of his childhood friend, Kim (later portrayed by Leven Rambin), that has fallen into the surf. Jay is saved from the surging waves by a crusty old surfer, Frosty Hesson (Gerard Butler). Two years later he reluctantly agrees to mentor Jay, after Jay persistently tells Frosty his unyielding desire to surf Mavericks. And so the adventure begins with Frosty putting Jay through a rigorous training regime, insisting that he must learn not only the basics of big wave riding, but must practice those skills that will help him survive the harrowing, unforgiving waves if he wipes out and finds himself in the grip of what’s called the “spin cycle.” Frosty also loans Jay his “big gun” long board. Jay’s single-parent mom (Elisabeth Shue) buys him a weather radio for his 16th birthday, allowing him to track the storms that produce the huge surf. Of course, after months of practice, the singular storm arrives and Jay’s opportunity presents itself. Mavericks is ready; however, will Jay be ready, and will he be able to master the mythical monsters that form and crash with a Zen-like intensity that must be seen to be believed? Meanwhile, Frosty and Kim stand on shore and watch Jay paddling toward his destiny. Chasing Mavericks. Streaming on HBO. Directed by Curtis Hanson. Starring Gerard Butler, Johnny Wesson, Elisabeth Shue. 1 hr., 56 min. Rated PG.

articles.text: Though Robert Redford’s film The Conspirator explores a footnote to history, one that is likely unfamiliar to most, it is also an allegory, which, perhaps not surprisingly, parallels recent post 9-11 events. Briefly, after Abraham Lincoln was assassinated at Ford’s Theater in Washington D.C., on the night of April 14, 1865, eight conspirators were eventually captured or killed, the most prominent being John Wilkes Booth, the actual assassin. What is not well known is that one of the people charged as an accomplice was Mary Surratt, a woman who ran a boarding house in Washington in which those accused, including her son, often met. She was accused of being the “woman who built the nest that hatched the plot.” Her trial was not held in a court before a jury of her peers, but before a military tribunal where the rules of evidence were either truncated or discarded altogether. The essence of the film is not the guilt or innocence of Mary Surratt, which remains to this day in doubt, but the fact that the government, reeling from the trauma of having lost a beloved president, was prepared to sacrifice due process and the Constitution in the interest of handing down swift justice. What makes this film compelling is the remarkable performance of Robin Wright as Mary Surratt. She is stoic and unyielding in her insistence that she is innocent, though she readily acknowledges that she is a Southerner who is anguished by the South’s defeat. Wright also manages to create a sense of ambiguity (something Redford surely intended) regarding what she might have known, or even agreed with, as her son and his cohorts planned the assassination. Cinematographer Newton Thomas Sigel captures the inevitability of Surratt’s situation as dust moats float through the thin light, and cigar smoke rises toward the courtroom ceiling. Many of the images are artful and lovely. From the outset the belief of all in the courtroom – the prosecution, members of the tribunal, even her defense attorney, portrayed nicely by James McAvoy – believe that the woman who sits before them is guilty, no matter the very thin circumstantial evidence offered by the government. But what the film also reveals is that most, such as Edwin Stanton, Secretary of War, played convincingly by Kevin Kline, were willing to sacrifice the Constitution while occluding the presumption of innocence, to achieve an end that they judged was in the best interest of the nation – though certainly not in the best interest of Mary Surratt. Of course, the parallels to America’s incarceration of those in the prison at Guantanamo, many held without the right of habeas corpus, the use of military tribunals, even torture, mirror what Redford so carefully creates in this film. The Civil War was concluded 150 years ago, and there are aspects still debated and discussed – which this film does so very well. Cicero said, “In times of war, the law falls silent.” It’s a line quoted by the prosecution while the government prepares Surratt’s final punishment. The Conspirator. Starring Robin Wright, James McAvoy, Tom Wilkinson, Evan Rachel Wood, Kevin Kline, and Danny Huston. Directed by Robert Redford. 2 hrs., 25 min. Rated PG-13

pages.text: 18 Wednesday, January 12, 2022 Features By Will Adams Part 35 in a biweekly series We just got back from a couple of weeks in one of our favorite places, Bucerias, Mexico. It is a quiet beach town, an alternative to the crowds, bustle and pressure of nearby Puerto Vallarta, 30 minutes to the south. At least it was. After a two-year COVID absence we were overwhelmed to find new construction everywhere. Not just construction, but radically different development, Development in danger of changing the entire sense of the town. For those who may be familiar with the place, even the beloved landmark Mark’s restaurant closed for good one week before we arrived. Is all lost? Experiencing this, it was impossible not to reflect on change in our built environment. New buildings, bigger buildings, old places of business gone, new ones in place, more traffic, more people – everything changing, like it or not. It is impossible to really keep things as they were in Bucerias, in the Bay Area, or in Piedmont. In fact, I suppose keeping things “the way they are” or “the way they were” is really a misconception. What this thought represents is really only a brief snapshot in time of what in reality is an ongoing continuous evolution. Sooner or later the continuous accumulation of even small changes become recognizable as something truly new and different. One of the great ironies of much development is that often the very things that made a place desirable and valuable in Drawings by Will Adams The 2 meter-wide iconic pedestrian “kissing bridge” in Bucerias. Mexico was used by hundreds of people each day and the magnificent nearby tree must be over 200 years old. On our two-year COVID deferred visit of a few weeks ago we discovered both are now gone. There is certainly a sense of loss, but we must hope they will be thoughtfully replaced by structures and landscaping of a kind that will inspire in the future. The historic town had a scale and aesthetic that exuded a feeling of peace and tranquility, but it couldn’t keep up with its own desirability. The current development will test the architectural, landscape and urban design competence of the Mexican architects, landscape architects and planners. The level of craftsmanship and artistry common throughout Mexico is evident everywhere. The resulting desirability has led to development, as more and more people want to experience the place. As a result, construction is suddenly everywhere. Note the rebar sticking out on top of the building, indicating that it will be yet higher than the drawing indicates. the first place are compromised or even destroyed by incompetent expansion. In other words, what inspired the development is itself lost as a result of the development. But is this always the case? The answer is no, not always. My thinking is that we have to be prepared for this inevitability of change, of development. We must be well-versed and educated enough to be able to judge early in the proposal and planning process what is good and what is bad – where we are going and where we want to go. For our own future environmental, aesthetic and indeed entire life style, we must manage and direct inevitable changes appropriately. articles.text: It was decided on Monday, January 3, that the members of the Piedmont Recreation Department’s First Mondays Reading Group would not be comfortable sitting outside the Tea House in Piedmont Park in 52-degree weather, so the group’s discussion that afternoon was changed to a Zoom call. In the warm comfort of their homes, there was a good turnout of 15 readers calling in. Participating were Mike Henn, Nancy Henn, Ken Young, Melba Yee, Lois Price, Sarah Johnson, Alicia Rivera, Laura Goldman, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Phil Witte, Dick Carter, and discussion leaders Carol Long and Priscilla Wanerus. The group was pleased to welcome first-time participant Pat McMahon for the discussion of their January read, Hamnet. Maggie O’Farrell’s Hamnet, published in 2020, received strong critical acclaim, and was named one of the five best works of fiction in 2020 by the New York Times Book Review. The book proved to be an excellent selection for the group. It was enjoyed by some readers, but less liked by others, so it made for a thought-provoking discussion. This historical novel takes place in Stratford-upon-Avon mostly in 1596, when Shakespeare’s only son, Hamnet, died at age 11 from the bubonic plague. Interestingly, O’Farrell’s story doesn’t focus on Shakespeare. He is only referred to as “the father,” “the Latin tutor,” or “her husband” throughout the book. Instead, it centers on his wife, Agnes, and their three children. The story initially covers Shakespeare’s unremarkable youth, problems with his family, his courtship of Agnes, her pregnancy, and their required marriage, before focusing on the circumstances and effects surrounding the boy’s death. Hamnet is a novel about the grief associated with the loss of a child and the damage done to those left behind. The novel has two timelines, before and after Hamnet’s death. The first chapters are devoted to Shakespeare’s coming-of-age with his struggle to cope with an abusive, drunkard grandfather and his early career as a teacher; and the chapters covering his years and events in London that are mostly not told to the reader. Maggie O’Farrell’s Hamnet was named one of the five best works of fiction in 2020 by the New York Times Book Review. In these later chapters the father transfers his grief into the creation of his masterpiece, Hamlet, titled with a common variant of his son’s name. Some members of the group thoroughly enjoyed O’Farrell’s work. They felt it was beautifully written and a powerful description of grief associated with loss. They found O’Farrell’s detailed writing captivating. An example of which is a remarkable 10-page passage in which she traces how the plague reached the Shakespeare children, starting with an infected flea on an African monkey in Alexandria, Egypt, and ending with the death of the boy. It was the “ultimate in contact tracing” for the readers. They also found it impressive that the author could make such a complete, imaginative story out of a character and situation where there is so little actual history known. Other readers were less enthusiastic about the book. They saw this as a story of family dynamics with not-very-interesting people. It was an easy read, but they didn’t have an emotional connection with the characters. They couldn’t quite put their fingers on what was missing for them. Some found the manipulation of events going back and forth to be confusing in the first part of the book. There seemed to be agreement that O’Farrell’s ending tied the story together, concluding that people handle grief in different ways. For future reads, the group had previously selected the non-fiction The Boys in the Boat by Daniel James Brown for February and the novel The Midnight Library by Matt Haig for March. Destiny of the Republic by Candice Millard was chosen as their April book. A 2011 bestseller, it is about the little known, but remarkable life of the assassinated President James Garfield. The group’s next discussion will be Monday, February 7 starting at 1:30 p.m. Weather and Covid protocols permitting, the group will meet in person at the Japanese Tea House by the Community Hall in Piedmont Park. If the forecast is for cold or rain, the group will have their discussion via a Zoom call. New readers are welcome to join the group, and there is no fee to participate. articles.text: January 5 was the first Wednesday of 2022 for the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays group. It was a 52 degree and overcast morning, but New Year’s resolutions may have been at work as a strong showing of 31 walkers showed up at the Exedra for the group’s normal 10:30 a.m. start. The group had largely achieved its annual goal of walking every safe Piedmont street during 2021, but there were a few that they had not been able to get to. One was the challenging Crest Road, a street that is difficult because it is long and steep. It is also far from the center of town. The walkers may have walked it in years past, but the current group couldn’t remember ever walking on Crest. They thought it would be a good hike and a great way to start 2022. Going on Highland Avenue the long line of walkers looked like a parade. They took their usual route to Hampton Park, going up Sheridan, Wildwood, and Crocker Avenues, and on to Hampton Road past Crocker Park. Crossing Highland to get on Sheridan required a bit of traffic control for this big group. Many of the walkers are also members of the Recreation Department’s First Mondays Reading Group, and some resumed their enjoyable conversation about their discussion on Monday about Hamnet, a best-seller by Maggie O’Farrell in 2020. As the group walked, they also noted discarded Christmas trees at street curbs, and some homes still decorated – happy reminders of the holidays. The walkers were pleased that an inflatable, moving Scoopy Doo and his friends were at the top of Hampton at Sotelo Avenue to wish them a New Year. The walkers continued on to Hampton Park, where members of the group preferring not to climb to the top of Crest were able to return to the middle of town. The group then crossed La Salle and passed through the two, large, white columns on both sides of Hampton that marked the main entrance to the large St. James Woods residential development of early Piedmont times. They noted the sidewalks’ brown tile inlays that marked this neighborhood’s extensive boundary. The walkers quickly came to Crest and started their ascent. The slope of the street’s initial portion is moderate, but it increases significantly over about a quarter mile as it nears Somerset Road. The group turned right on Somerset, but the degree of hike difficulty didn’t diminish. A large, modern, multi-floor, white house with a metal gate blocking a steep driveway caught their attention. The house is high up the hillside and almost looks like a fortress overlooking a valley. The hearty band of walkers pressed on, looking for a path on the right side of the street that an old Piedmont city map said would take them down to Huntleigh Road. The path no longer seems to exist. After another half mile, they emerged on Estates Drive. The cloudy view of Oakland and the Bay was beautiful, and, some felt, maybe even worth the extra walk effort. However, it was time to return to the Exedra. A direct route down Estates Drive to the equally steep upper portion of Hampton Road was taken. The group then retraced their steps from Hampton Park to the center of town. They passed more reindeer, silver bells, and other holiday decorations as they went, and arrived only 10 minutes later than anticipated at the Community Center parking lot. They had covered over four miles of challenging, steep, and little-seen streets, and it was a good Walking on Wednesdays start for 2022. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday, rain or shine, at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https:// tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. Members of Walking on Wednesdays paused at Piedmont Park for a photo before ascending nearby Crest Road. On hand were: Tami DeSellier, Dena Belinkoff, Christine Calliste, Phil Witte, Stella Houston, Jim Kellogg, Siow Fang Tan, Noemi Alvarado, Brenda Ferrero, Mike Henn, Pat Sheehan, Nancy Henn, Alicia Rivera, Renee Goldhammer, Quincy Dong, Helen Dong, Priscilla Wanerus, Lois Price, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Lilly Guardia Labar, Melba Yee, Sherry Jacobs, Adrienne Hamlin, Alan Goldhammer, Harriette Louie, Pat McMahon, Jim Kuo, Pat Keller, and Dick Carter. The group was pleased to welcome first time walkers Carol Braves and Aaron Katzel.
