The first chapters are devoted to Shakespeare’s coming-of-age with his struggle to cope with an abusive, drunkard grandfather and his early career as a teacher; and the chapters covering his years and events in London that are mostly not told to the reader. Maggie O’Farrell’s Hamnet was named one of the five best works of fiction in 2020 by the New York Times Book Review. In these later chapters the father transfers his grief into the creation of his masterpiece, Hamlet, titled with a common variant of his son’s name. Some members of the group thoroughly enjoyed O’Farrell’s work. They felt it was beautifully written and a powerful description of grief associated with loss. They found O’Farrell’s detailed writing captivating. An example of which is a remarkable 10-page passage in which she traces how the plague reached the Shakespeare children, starting with an infected flea on an African monkey in Alexandria, Egypt, and ending with the death of the boy. It was the “ultimate in contact tracing” for the readers. They also found it impressive that the author could make such a complete, imaginative story out of a character and situation where there is so little actual history known. Other readers were less enthusiastic about the book. They saw this as a story of family dynamics with not-very-interesting people. It was an easy read, but they didn’t have an emotional connection with the characters. They couldn’t quite put their fingers on what was missing for them. Some found the manipulation of events going back and forth to be confusing in the first part of the book. There seemed to be agreement that O’Farrell’s ending tied the story together, concluding that people handle grief in different ways. It was a 52 degree and overcast morning, but New Year’s resolutions may have been at work as a strong showing of 31 walkers showed up at the Exedra for the group’s normal 10:30 a.m. start. The group had largely achieved its annual goal of walking every safe Piedmont street during 2021, but there were a few that they had not been able to get to. One was the challenging Crest Road, a street that is difficult because it is long and steep. It is also far from the center of town. The walkers may have walked it in years past, but the current group couldn’t remember ever walking on Crest. They thought it would be a good hike and a great way to start 2022. Going on Highland Avenue the long line of walkers looked like a parade. They took their usual route to Hampton Park, going up Sheridan, Wildwood, and Crocker Avenues, and on to Hampton Road past Crocker Park. Crossing Highland to get on Sheridan required a bit of traffic control for this big group. Many of the walkers are also members of the Recreation Department’s First Mondays Reading Group, and some resumed their enjoyable conversation about their discussion on Monday about Hamnet, a best-seller by Maggie O’Farrell in 2020. As the group walked, they also noted discarded Christmas trees at street curbs, and some homes still decorated – happy reminders of the holidays. The walkers were pleased that an inflatable, moving Scoopy Doo and his friends were at the top of Hampton at Sotelo Avenue to wish them a New Year. The walkers continued on to Hampton Park, where members of the group preferring not to climb to the top of Crest were able to return to the middle of town. The group then crossed La Salle and passed through the two, large, white columns on both sides of Hampton that marked the main entrance to the large St. James Woods residential development of early Piedmont times. They noted the sidewalks’ brown tile inlays that marked this neighborhood’s extensive boundary. The walkers quickly came to Crest and started their ascent. The slope of the street’s initial portion is moderate, but it increases significantly over about a quarter mile as it nears Somerset Road. The group turned right on Somerset, but the degree of hike difficulty didn’t diminish. A large, modern, multi-floor, white house with a metal gate blocking a steep driveway caught their attention. The house is high up the hillside and almost looks like a fortress overlooking a valley. The hearty band of walkers pressed on, looking for a path on the right side of the street that an old Piedmont city map said would take them down to Huntleigh Road. The path no longer seems to exist. articles.text: Nat Dodge, a resident of Piedmont for more than 50 years and a fourth generation Piedmonter, passed away at home on February 4, 2020. The onset of Covid prevented the family from holding a memorial service at that time. Born Nathaniel S. Dodge III in Oakland on August 10, 1937, he was the son of Elinor and Nathaniel Dodge Jr. and was raised in Orinda when it was still considered “the country.” He attended Orinda Union Grammar School where, in the fourth grade, he met his future wife, Janis Armstrong. Nat graduated from Acalanes High School in Lafayette in 1955 where he was a member of the football team, and track & field team in discus and shot put. He also drew cartoons and illustrations for the school publications. He attended the University of California at Davis where he played football, was on the Student Council, and was President of the Sigma Nu Fraternity. He graduated in January 1960. He and Jan were married six months earlier on June 13, 1959. A member of the Army ROTC, upon graduation he was commissioned as a 2nd Lieutenant in the Army. Before he was posted to the Infantry School at Fort Benning, Georgia, Nat and his bride of six months went on a wonderful three-month driving tour of Europe in their Morris Minor. Nat retired after six years in the Army Reserve with the rank of Captain. Nat and Jan moved to Piedmont in 1966 and raised their two children. Nat worked at the American Rubber Manufacturing Co., a family business which manufactured rubber goods including conveyor belts, and fire and wine hose. In 1984, Nat left the business and started Dodge Co., Inc., a consulting firm specializing in the design and supply of process equipment to the mining industry. The primary focus was on copper and precious metal mines that were expanding around the world. The company participated in projects in Uzbekistan, West Africa, North and South America, Indonesia, and Australia. Associate offices were established in the U.K., Chile, and Singapore to better serve and support clients in remote project sites. Nat was a longtime member of the American Association of Mining Engineers (AIME), the Nevada Mining Association, and the Sociedad Nacional Mineria de Chile. Nat Dodge, a resident of Piedmont since 1966, passed away on February 4, 2020. Nat was an avid outdoorsman. He was a fair wing shot, fly fisherman, horseman, skier, sailor, and a (very) frustrated golfer. He was an accomplished artist, a collector of old and rare books, and a great reader. He enjoyed both classical and country music, good wine, good food, and spirited political conversations. He was a member of Claremont Country Club and served for several years on the club’s History Committee. Over the years he served the City of Piedmont as a member of the Recreation Commission, and coached a number of his son Nat’s youth sports teams. In recent years, Nat and Jan were able to spend more time at the family property in Northwest Sonoma County, which has served as a family retreat and provided the simple beauty and quiet lifestyle he loved so much. The ranch allowed him to pass on to his children and grandchildren an appreciation of the outdoors, and the basics of hard work, responsibility, and the joy of a job well done. Nat is survived by Jan, his best friend and devoted wife of 60 years, and by his two children, son Nat IV and wife Sallie of Boulder, Colorado, and daughter Beth Dodge Weaver and husband Thad of Wilmington, Delaware. He is also survived by five grandchildren, Robert Weaver of Santa Rosa; Jack Weaver of Morgantown, West Virginia; Henry Dodge of Denver, Colorado; Louisa Dodge of New York City; and Nathaniel Dodge of Jackson, Wyoming. A private family graveside service was held at Mountain View Cemetery in Oakland.

articles.text: Dear Abby: Have you heard about the recent thefts of Frenchies? I am worried. I would not want to lose Tank. He is quite the cutie. Have there been any dog thefts in Piedmont? - Jen and Tank the French Bull Dog Dear Jen and Tank: Fortunately, I have not heard of any Frenchies being taken in Piedmont, but I have heard sad stories in San Francisco and Oakland. Our pug was stolen in the East Bay Hills when she was with a dog walker. By the grace of God (and a big reward offered), she was returned. It was agony, and I wouldn’t want it to happen to anyone. Here are some tips to consider for keeping your dog safe: 1. Get your dog chipped. In years past, chip reading was not universal but now it is. Most vets can read any type of chip. 2. Take a lot of photos of your dog (with and without you) and keep them on your phone so you can send them quickly to various dog services. Home Again is one service that sends out alerts quickly of lost pets with photos to shelters and vet clinics. 3. Do not share too much about your walks on social media. Apparently, some people may track you if they want a dog. 4. Always have a collar with tags on the dog. Even though you are watching them, sometimes they can sneak away. A tag can save a lot of anguish. 5. Be aware of your surroundings. If you get the feeling that Tank is being a bit too rambunctious and may get lost while he’s playing, take him home. Or if you feel someone is watching you, don’t dismiss it. 6. Some vets recommend getting your pet ‘tattooed.’ It can be done under general anesthesia when you’re having the dog neutered. The tattoo will be a seven letter and digit combo that will be unique to each pet and placed in the right ear. Apparently, it can be easily traced and is a permanent way to help get pets back to their owners. Sounds a little painful, but if they’re under anesthesia anyway, they won’t feel a thing. Wags to you and Tank. -Abby Dear Abby: We rescued a bleeding white husky on Christmas Day in the rain near the reservoir on Blair Avenue. Andrew Jackson – “Old Hickory Nuts” himself – battling indigenous peoples on what is now the Rose Garden. Yes, the lives of our most famous presidents consist almost entirely of myths. The nineteenth century is generally considered by many thoughtful people to be the Golden Age of Myths. Our presidents of that era are presumably the most mythical. As just one example, James Garfield’s beard was said to be so thick, it could stop a bullet. Sadly, how wrong. Myths, indeed, can kill. Teddy Roosevelt knew the power of myth. He founded the Bull Moose Party, based on a mythical animal comprised of two real animals. Instead of the usual presidential portrait, he commissioned a bust of himself carved onto the face of Mount Rushmore. His critics, known as “bust busters,” attacked him for self-mythologizing, but he, like Muhammad’s mountain (there’s a reference you don’t hear much anymore), would not budge. Three lesser Presidents were added later, diluting the whole effect, but Teddy, a great outdoorsman and an early environmentalist, was pleased with his enormous visage adorning a previously pristine granite cliff, though he was annoyed at himself for neglecting to remove his glasses while sitting for the sculptor. Barack Obama is commonly believed to be this country’s first African-American president. Not so. The first African-American president was Thomas Jefferson’s mistress, Sally Hemings. She briefly served as head of state and commander in chief when Jefferson became incapacitated during a three-day Bordeaux bender. When he came to, he purportedly snarled at her, “Who told you to go and purchase the Louisiana Territory?” George Washington was mythical even before he became president. He threw a dollar across the Washington River, later named the Potomac. How the Nationals could use an arm like that now! Some myths beg exploding. Take the myth of Honest Abe. Lyin’ Lincoln is more like it. He frequently fibbed – to his friends, to his family, to Congress, to people he didn’t even know. When caught in one of his many deceits, Lincoln would smile that big Lincolnesque grin and say, “Just joshin’!” Such a cunning man. “How’s that Gettysburg Address coming along, Mr. President?” “Almost done,” the Great Equivocator would reply. “On page 40 now.” Then he would wait until the last minute and scribble some words on the back of an envelope. Benjamin Franklin was another early American who wallowed in myths – the roller skate key in the thunderstorm experiment, the Poor Richard stories he told to attract a certain type of woman, the coonskin cap that was really a muskrat cap – all helped to create the myth that he was once president. Yet, he never was, losing narrowly in the disputed 1798 election to Alexander Hamilton. Some myths have faded over time. Mention the great Grover Cleveland Cloning Incident of the late 1880s and many people, even school librarians, scratch their heads, and not because of lice. Cleveland, our twenty-second president (“Cleveland 22”), was so anxious that he might not win reelection that he allowed himself to be cloned, so that he could accomplish twice as much and secure a lasting legacy. The cloning procedure, called homo-hectography in those days, was primitive by today’s standards and so time-consuming that Benjamin Harrison became the twenty-third president before the cloned Cleveland (“Cleveland 24”) could take office. articles.text: Bonita Avenue School was Piedmont’s first public school, built in 1909 and designed by Albert Farr. The first order of business was to build a city hall and a school. While the Board of Trustees debated the location of City Hall (some wanted it on Highland Avenue), plans progressed for Piedmont’s first public school. The Bonita Avenue School was built in 1909. It had 8 classrooms for 8 teachers who taught 8 grades and 318 students. The Lake School (now the Egbert W. Beach School) on Lake Avenue) was built three years later to provide more classrooms for students. The first school was built on the east side of Bonita Avenue between Oakland and Vista Avenues, hence the name, Bonita Avenue School. When Frank C. Havens died in 1918, the school was renamed in his memory. Albert Farr designed the school in the Spanish Colonial or Spanish Mission design that he would use the following year for Piedmont’s City Hall and the Oakland Avenue Bridge. The school had two large, square Spanish towers with shallow balconies and ornate cupolas on each side of the main building. Classroom wings on each side extended to the front and rear, making the building an H-shape with the school’s entry set between the two wings. Large arched windows flanked the arched entry, and Mission tile covered the roofs and capped the walls to the courtyard entry. Clara Crumpton was the first principal of the Bonita Avenue School and taught first grade. On the occasion of the Panama-Pacific International Exposition in San Francisco in 1915, Miss Crumpton had her students recreate the “Tower of Jewels” in front of the school. In 1910 Ellen Driscoll began teaching at the school, and became principal of Havens School from 1920 to 1940. She was a popular teacher and was known for her keen memory as a principal. She knew the names of each of her 300 students. The 1947 photo shows the school with its courtyard and classroom wings. The long, rectangular building at the rear is a 5-classroom addition completed in 1937 by the Federal government as a Work Projects Administration project. In 1940 the Board of Education contracted again with the WPA to build auditoriums for what by then were three elementary schools. The auditorium at Havens was dedicated as the Ellen Driscoll Playhouse. articles.text: The April 18, 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire sent thousands of San Franciscans fleeing to the East Bay. The fires and smoke were visible for days from the Piedmont hills as over 15,000 lost their homes in the fire. While there were no reports of refugees camping in Piedmont Park, some refugees did stay with friends in Piedmont. As Oakland looked to the hills to annex more land for this influx of earthquake survivors, a group of far-sighted Piedmont residents did not want Piedmont to become part of Oakland. Hugh Craig and James Ballentine immediately began an effort to incorporate Piedmont as a city. They quickly drew up a map of Piedmont’s borders using an existing Piedmont Sanitary District map and filed the map in Sacramento. On January 26, 1907, Piedmonters voted to incorporate. The vote passed, and Piedmont officially became a municipality four days later, January 30, 1907. A photo from 1926 shows Ellen Driscoll, then the principal of Havens School, with her students. Under the guidance of Clara Crumpton, the first principal of the Bonita Avenue School, students recreated the Tower of Jewels, the centerpiece of the 1915 Panama-Pacific International Exposition in San Francisco.

articles.text: In Piedmont, we are faced with many of the same issues, pressures, dangers, and fortunately, possibilities – just like the rest of the state, country and world. The main question is. what are the models for us going forward? What do we emulate? What do we avoid, reject? Many things are possible…. except standing still. We have to be aware of our built environment, how it was formed, and why it is successful or unsuccessful. In short, we have to be educated. We also have to involve the young people – the next generation – in this awareness and process. Sooner than we realize they will be the driving force that forms our environmental and resulting cultural future.
